claim: Actin is a DAMP detected in mammals by the receptor DNGR-1, expressed by dendritic cells.
source: Actin is a DAMP detected in mammals by the receptor, DNGR-1, expressed by dendritic cells (DCs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction.

claim: DNGR-1 is phosphorylated by Src-family kinases.
source: DNGR-1 is phosphorylated by Src-family kinases and recruits the tyrosine kinase Syk to promote DC cross-presentation of dead cell-associated antigens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DNGR-1 recruits the tyrosine kinase Syk to promote DC cross-presentation of dead cell-associated antigens.
source: DNGR-1 is phosphorylated by Src-family kinases and recruits the tyrosine kinase Syk to promote DC cross-presentation of dead cell-associated antigens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Administration of actin to Drosophila melanogaster triggers a response characterised by selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body.
source: Administration of actin to Drosophila melanogaster triggers a response characterised by selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body through the cytokine Upd3 and its JAK/STAT-coupled receptor, Domeless.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The actin-induced response in Drosophila occurs through the cytokine Upd3 and its JAK/STAT-coupled receptor, Domeless.
source: Administration of actin to Drosophila melanogaster triggers a response characterised by selective induction of STAT target genes in the fat body through the cytokine Upd3 and its JAK/STAT-coupled receptor, Domeless.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The actin-induced response in Drosophila requires signalling via Shark, the Drosophila orthologue of Syk.
source: Notably, this response requires signalling via Shark, the Drosophila orthologue of Syk, and Src42A, a Drosophila Src-family kinase, and is dependent on Nox activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The actin-induced response in Drosophila requires Src42A, a Drosophila Src-family kinase.
source: Notably, this response requires signalling via Shark, the Drosophila orthologue of Syk, and Src42A, a Drosophila Src-family kinase, and is dependent on Nox activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The actin-induced response in Drosophila is dependent on Nox activity.
source: Notably, this response requires signalling via Shark, the Drosophila orthologue of Syk, and Src42A, a Drosophila Src-family kinase, and is dependent on Nox activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Extracellular actin detection via a Src-family kinase-dependent cascade is an ancient means of detecting cell injury that precedes the evolution of adaptive immunity.
source: Thus, extracellular actin detection via a Src-family kinase-dependent cascade is an ancient means of detecting cell injury that precedes the evolution of adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing conserved signalling components between flies and mammals.

claim: Actin injection led to the differential expression of 241 genes at 3 hr, 1297 genes at 6 hr and 351 genes at 24 hr post-injection.
source: Actin injection led to the differential expression of a large number of genes as compared to injection of buffer control: 241 genes were induced or repressed at 3 hr, 1297 genes at 6 hr and 351 genes at 24 hr post-injection (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: Among genes induced selectively in actin treated flies are members of the Tot gene family including TotM, TotA and TotC, as well as Socs36E, Diedel and Tep1.
source: Notably, among genes that were induced selectively in actin treated flies, we found the members of the Tot gene family including TotM, TotA and TotC, as well as Socs36E, Diedel and thioester-containing protein (Tep)1 (Figure 1b, c), all of which are STAT-dependent (Boutros et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2005; Lagueux et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data in Figure 1b and 1c, and by citations to prior work showing these genes are STAT-dependent.

claim: TotM, TotA, TotC, Socs36E, Diedel and Tep1 are STAT-dependent genes.
source: Notably, among genes that were induced selectively in actin treated flies, we found the members of the Tot gene family including TotM, TotA and TotC, as well as Socs36E, Diedel and thioester-containing protein (Tep)1 (Figure 1b, c), all of which are STAT-dependent (Boutros et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2005; Lagueux et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Boutros et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2005; Lagueux et al., 2000).

claim: Target genes of STAT92E were highly enriched in actin- compared to buffer-injected flies.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of published datasets confirmed that target genes of STAT92E were highly enriched in actin- compared to buffer-injected flies (Figure 1d) (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figure 1d with a p-value < 0.0001.

claim: STAT responsive elements are present in promoters of genes upregulated by actin but not buffer injection.
source: The presence of STAT binding sites in promoters of genes upregulated by actin but not buffer injection was validated by bioinformatics analyses (STAT responsive elements: p=7.8×10–4 using Transfac database, p=1.63×10–8 using JASPAR database).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analyses using Transfac and JASPAR databases with significant p-values.

claim: Actin but not buffer injection potently triggers expression of Tot, Tep and Diedel genes peaking at 24 hr after injection.
source: We confirmed by RT-qPCR that actin but not buffer injection potently triggers expression of Tot, Tep and Diedel genes peaking at 24 hr after injection (Figure 2a-f and data not shown).
evidence: This is confirmed by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2a-f.

claim: Actin injection did not lead to the expression of the AMP genes Drs and Dpt.
source: Actin injection did not lead to the expression of the AMP genes Drs and Dpt, which were induced only upon experimental fungal or bacterial infection (Figure 2g, h).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2g and 2h showing no induction of Drs and Dpt by actin.

claim: The absence of Drs and Dpt induction by actin indicates the absence of microbial contaminants in actin preparations.
source: This indicates the absence of microbial contaminants in actin preparations and demonstrates that the response to actin differs from that to septic injury, in which induction of STAT targets is invariably accompanied by that of genes downstream of Toll or Imd (Agaisse et al., 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Brun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of AMP gene induction and supported by citations to prior work on septic injury responses.

claim: The response to actin differs from that to septic injury, in which induction of STAT targets is invariably accompanied by that of genes downstream of Toll or Imd.
source: This indicates the absence of microbial contaminants in actin preparations and demonstrates that the response to actin differs from that to septic injury, in which induction of STAT targets is invariably accompanied by that of genes downstream of Toll or Imd (Agaisse et al., 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Brun et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the data showing selective STAT target induction without AMP induction, and by citations to prior work.

claim: TotM induction by actin was much greater than that elicited by injury (clean or septic) or by heat shock.
source: In this regard, TotM induction by actin was much greater than that elicited by injury (clean or septic) or by heat shock, which are classically regarded as inducers of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway (Agaisse et al., 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a comparing TotM induction across different stimuli.

claim: The response to actin did not require microbiota or their products.
source: Finally, actin injection induced equivalent TotM levels in germ-free and SPF (specific pathogen free) flies, showing that microbiota or their products do not contribute to the response, despite the fact that they are inevitably introduced into the thorax of SPF flies upon piercing of the cuticle during injection (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2i showing equivalent TotM induction in germ-free and SPF flies.

claim: The response to actin did not require Wolbachia.
source: Similarly, the response to actin did not require Wolbachia, a genus of vertically-transmitted intracellular bacteria that infect many arthropods and is known to impact immune responses (Teixeira et al., 2008; Hedges et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2i and citations to prior work on Wolbachia.

claim: The introduction of actin into the haemolymph of flies uniquely induces a sterile inflammatory response characterised by selective induction of STAT target genes.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the introduction of actin into the haemolymph of flies uniquely induces a sterile inflammatory response characterised by selective induction of STAT target genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective STAT target induction without AMP induction or requirement for microbiota.

claim: TotM induction could be observed upon injection of as little as 0.1 ng actin, which corresponds to the contents of 8–10 cells.
source: However, TotM induction could be observed upon injection of as little as 0.1 ng actin, which corresponds to the contents of 8–10 cells, thereby underscoring physiological relevance (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 2j.

claim: Actin from all tested species (human, rabbit and Drosophila) induced TotM.
source: Actin from all tested species (human, rabbit and Drosophila) induced TotM (see Materials and Methods), consistent with the extreme evolutionary conservation of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the text and is consistent with the known conservation of actin.

claim: TotM induction was not due to the cytopathic effects of actin filaments in vivo as the response was triggered equally by phalloidin-stabilised F-actin or latrunculin-stabilised G-actin.
source: Importantly, TotM induction was not due to the cytopathic effects of actin filaments in vivo as the response was triggered equally by phalloidin-stabilised filamentous (F)- or latrunculin-stabilised globular (G)-actin (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2k showing equivalent TotM induction by F-actin and G-actin.

claim: Injection of a non-polymerisable G-actin mutant induced a response equivalent to that triggered by an injection of polymeric F-actin.
source: Injection of the G-actin mutant induced a response equivalent to that triggered by an injection of polymeric F-actin (Figure 2l).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2l comparing the G-actin mutant to F-actin.

claim: STAT target gene expression was enriched in regions containing the fat body.
source: Analysis of physically-dissected body parts of w1118 flies injected with actin revealed that STAT target gene expression was enriched in regions containing the fat body (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3a showing TotM expression in dissected tissues.

claim: Injection of actin, but not mock injection or injection of buffer alone, resulted in a time-dependent increase in GFP fluorescence exclusively in Tomato+ fat body cells.
source: Injection of actin, but not mock injection (0 hr) or injection of buffer alone, resulted in a time-dependent increase in GFP fluorescence exclusively in Tomato+ fat body cells (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 3b and quantification in Figure 3c.

claim: Overexpression of dome ΔCyt2.3 in the whole fly using a ubiquitous Actin-Gal4 driver resulted in significant attenuation of TotM expression in response to actin injection.
source: First, we validated the requirement for the JAK/STAT pathway by expressing a dominant negative Domeless receptor (dome ΔCyt2.3). Overexpression of dome ΔCyt2.3 in the whole fly using a ubiquitous Actin-Gal4 driver resulted in significant attenuation of TotM expression in response to actin injection (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing reduced TotM expression with dome ΔCyt2.3 overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of dome ΔCyt2.3 specifically in the fat body using a fat body-restricted, temperature-sensitive c564-Gal80ts driver resulted in significant attenuation of TotM expression in response to actin injection.
source: The same result was obtained when overexpressing dome ΔCyt2.3 specifically in the fat body using a fat body-restricted, temperature-sensitive c564-Gal80ts driver (c564-Gal4; Tub-Gal80ts) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4a showing reduced TotM expression with fat body-specific dome ΔCyt2.3 overexpression.

claim: The response was attenuated in extracts of flies in which STAT signalling was reduced by overexpressing the STAT inhibitor, dPIAS, in the fat body.
source: Concordant with those results, the response was also attenuated in extracts of flies in which STAT signalling was reduced by overexpressing the STAT inhibitor, dPIAS, in the fat body using two different fat body-specific drivers under the control or not of a Gal80ts temperature-sensitive repressor (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4b and 4c showing reduced TotM expression with dPIAS overexpression.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of STAT92E specifically in fat body cells was sufficient to suppress TotM induction by injected actin.
source: Finally, RNAi-mediated knockdown of STAT92E specifically in fat body cells was sufficient to suppress TotM induction by injected actin (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4d showing suppressed TotM expression with STAT92E knockdown.

claim: Canonical STAT-dependent TotM induction in the fat body accounts for the global response seen in total fly extracts.
source: These results suggest that canonical STAT-dependent TotM induction in the fat body accounts for the global response seen in total fly extracts.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments showing that fat body-specific manipulation of STAT signalling affects the global TotM response.

claim: Ablation of STAT92E in the fat body did not alter the inducibility of some of the other most highly upregulated genes in actin-injected flies.
source: Although we focused on TotM, we also assessed whether some of the other most highly upregulated genes in actin-injected flies were similarly STAT-dependent. However, ablation of STAT92E in the fat body did not alter the inducibility of those we tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Actin-induced downregulation of some tested transcripts was prevented by reduction of STAT92E in the fat body.
source: In contrast, actin-induced downregulation of some tested transcripts was prevented by reduction of STAT92E in the fat body (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: STAT activation is a major outcome of actin injection but extracellular actin likely triggers additional signalling pathways.
source: These data, together with the GSEA analysis, underscore the notion that STAT activation is a major outcome of actin injection but suggest that extracellular actin likely triggers additional signalling pathways, which may or not involve the fat body and impact gene expression and/or transcript stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that not all actin-induced gene expression changes are STAT-dependent.

claim: Upd3 produced by haemocytes is essential to induce STAT responses in the fat body or in the intestine of flies subjected to septic injury or a high fat diet.
source: Upd3 produced by haemocytes is essential to induce STAT responses in the fat body or in the intestine of flies subjected to septic injury or a high fat diet (Agaisse et al., 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Woodcock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Agaisse et al., 2003; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Woodcock et al., 2015).

claim: Despite the near-complete elimination of haemocytes, TotM induction in response to actin in UAS-rpr flies was indistinguishable from that in controls.
source: Despite the near-complete elimination of haemocytes, TotM induction in response to actin in UAS-rpr flies was indistinguishable from that in controls (Figure 5c), indicating that haemocytes are redundant.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5c showing equivalent TotM induction in haemocyte-ablated and control flies.

claim: Haemocyte-derived Upd3 is dispensable for the TotM response to actin.
source: We further established that haemocyte-derived Upd3 is dispensable by using a upd3 RNAi line crossed to another line carrying a Hemolectin-Gal4 driver (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5d showing that haemocyte-specific Upd3 knockdown does not affect TotM induction.

claim: Loss of the TotM response to actin injection was seen when the upd3 RNAi line was crossed to a line bearing a r4-Gal4 fat body driver.
source: We therefore tested the possibility that Upd3 might be essential but made by fat body cells themselves rather than haemocytes. Consistent with that notion, loss of the TotM response to actin injection was seen when the upd3 RNAi line was crossed to a line bearing a r4-Gal4 fat body driver (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5d showing loss of TotM induction with fat body-specific Upd3 knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of Upd1 and Upd2 in fat body cells had no effect on the response to actin.
source: In contrast to Upd3, knockdown of Upd1 and Upd2 in fat body cells had no effect on the response to actin (Figure 5e), confirming Upd3 as the key cytokine.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5e showing that Upd1 and Upd2 knockdown does not affect TotM induction.

claim: Extracellular actin leads to Upd3 production by fat body cells, which acts in an autocrine or paracrine fashion via Domeless to induce STAT activation and induction of STAT response genes.
source: We conclude that extracellular actin leads to Upd3 production by fat body cells, which acts in an autocrine or paracrine fashion via Domeless to induce STAT activation and induction of STAT response genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments showing that fat body-derived Upd3 is required for the response.

claim: Conditional silencing of Shark in adult flies using a ubiquitous driver led to a significant reduction in TotM expression upon actin injection.
source: Indeed, conditional silencing of Shark in adult flies using a ubiquitous driver led to a significant reduction in TotM expression upon actin injection (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6a showing reduced TotM expression with ubiquitous Shark knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of Shark within the fat body using a c564-Gal80ts driver led to a large reduction in the levels of actin-induced TotM in total flies.
source: Next, we asked whether the fat body itself might be the primary site of Shark signalling. Consistent with that notion, knockdown of Shark within the fat body using a c564-Gal80ts driver led to a large reduction in the levels of actin-induced TotM in total flies that had been shifted to the restrictive temperature (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6b showing reduced TotM expression with fat body-specific Shark knockdown.

claim: Silencing of the Src family kinase Src42A using a ubiquitous temperature-sensitive driver led to a striking reduction in actin-induced TotM levels.
source: Shark activation occurs downstream of Src family kinase activity (Ziegenfuss et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2015). Silencing of the Src family kinase Src42A using a ubiquitous temperature-sensitive driver also led to a striking reduction in actin-induced TotM levels (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing reduced TotM expression with ubiquitous Src42A knockdown, and by citations to prior work.

claim: Src42A was specifically required in the fat body because silencing with fat body-specific drivers led to complete loss of actin-induced TotM.
source: As for Shark, Src42A was specifically required in the fat body because silencing with fat body-specific drivers also led to complete loss of actin-induced TotM (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6d showing loss of TotM induction with fat body-specific Src42A knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of a dominant negative allele of Src42A using an ubiquitous or fat body-specific driver led to a marked reduction in actin-driven TotM levels.
source: In keeping with the knockdown data, overexpression of a dominant negative allele of Src42A (Src42ADN) using an ubiquitous or fat body-specific driver similarly led to a marked reduction in actin-driven TotM levels (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6e showing reduced TotM expression with Src42ADN overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of a constitutively active form of Src42A within the fat body was sufficient to induce a TotM response that was comparable in magnitude to that induced by actin injection.
source: Finally, the overexpression of a constitutively active form of Src42A within the fat body was sufficient to induce a TotM response that was comparable in magnitude to that induced by actin injection (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6f showing TotM induction with constitutively active Src42A.

claim: Drpr null mutants displayed a reduced TotM response to actin injection.
source: We found that drpr null mutants displayed a reduced TotM response to actin injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The reduction in TotM response in drpr null mutants was not specific to Draper loss as it could not be rescued by complementation.
source: However, this reduction was not specific to Draper loss as it could not be rescued by complementation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and 1c showing lack of rescue.

claim: Conditional RNAi-mediated knockdown of drpr in the fat body had no effect on the TotM response to actin.
source: Consistent with that finding, conditional RNAi-mediated knockdown of drpr in the fat body had no effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Expression of Src42A and Shark in the fat body, but not of Draper, are essential for the response to extracellular actin.
source: We conclude that expression of Src42A and Shark in the fat body, but not of Draper, are essential for the response to extracellular actin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments showing requirement for Src42A and Shark but not Draper.

claim: Src family kinases are redox sensitive.
source: Src family kinases are redox sensitive (Giannoni et al., 2005) and can be activated by wound-derived H2O2 in both zebrafish and Drosophila (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Giannoni et al., 2005; Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).

claim: Src family kinases can be activated by wound-derived H2O2 in both zebrafish and Drosophila.
source: Src family kinases are redox sensitive (Giannoni et al., 2005) and can be activated by wound-derived H2O2 in both zebrafish and Drosophila (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).

claim: Conditional expression of cytoplasmic superoxide dismutase (Sod) ubiquitously or in the fat body diminished TotM induction by injected actin.
source: Consistent with a requirement for superoxide in the response to extracellular actin, conditional expression of cytoplasmic superoxide dismutase (Sod) (Missirlis et al., 2003) ubiquitously or in the fat body diminished TotM induction by injected actin (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7a showing reduced TotM expression with Sod overexpression, and by a citation to prior work.

claim: Conditional knockdown of Duox in the fat body of adult flies had no effect on the TotM response to injected actin.
source: Conditional knockdown of Duox in the fat body of adult flies had no effect on the TotM response to injected actin (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7b showing no effect of Duox knockdown.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Nox completely abrogated TotM induction, especially when using the c564 fat body-restricted driver.
source: In contrast, RNAi-mediated knockdown of Nox completely abrogated TotM induction, especially when using the c564 fat body-restricted driver (Figure 7c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7c and 7d showing loss of TotM induction with Nox knockdown.

claim: Extracellular actin leads to Nox activity in the fat body, which causes oxidation-dependent activation of Src42A and phosphorylation and activation of downstream targets, including Shark.
source: Together, these data suggest that extracellular actin leads to Nox activity in the fat body, which causes oxidation-dependent activation of Src42A and phosphorylation and activation of downstream targets, including Shark.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments showing requirement for Nox, Src42A, and Shark.

claim: Septic injury of adult flies leads to JAK/STAT activation and TotM induction in the fat body.
source: Previous studies have shown that septic injury of adult flies leads to JAK/STAT activation and TotM induction in the fat body (Brun et al., 2006; Agaisse et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brun et al., 2006; Agaisse et al., 2003).

claim: Septic injury with either Escherichia coli or Micrococcus luteus resulted in rapid accumulation of actin in the haemolymph of infected flies but not mock controls.
source: Using a model of septic injury with either Escherichia coli or Micrococcus luteus, we found rapid accumulation of actin in the haemolymph of infected flies but not mock (uninfected) controls (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 8a showing actin in haemolymph after septic injury.

claim: Septic injury was accompanied by the induction of TotM.
source: As previously described, septic injury was accompanied by the induction of TotM (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8b showing TotM induction after septic injury.

claim: Knockdown of Nox in the fat body led to roughly a 40% reduction in TotM after septic injury.
source: Strikingly, knockdown of Nox in the fat body led to roughly a 40% reduction in TotM while knockdown of Src42A completely abrogated the response (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8b showing reduced TotM expression with Nox knockdown after septic injury.

claim: Knockdown of Src42A in the fat body completely abrogated the TotM response to septic injury.
source: Strikingly, knockdown of Nox in the fat body led to roughly a 40% reduction in TotM while knockdown of Src42A completely abrogated the response (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8b showing loss of TotM induction with Src42A knockdown after septic injury.

claim: Expression of the Toll- or Imd-regulated AMPs, Dpt and Drs, was unaltered by Nox or Src42A knockdown in the fat body after septic injury.
source: Importantly, expression of the Toll- or and Imd-regulated AMPs, Dpt and Drs, was unaltered by Nox or Src42A knockdown in the fat body (Figure 8c, d).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8c and 8d showing no effect of Nox or Src42A knockdown on Dpt and Drs expression.

claim: Actin released into the haemolymph after septic injury can trigger JAK/STAT activation in the fat body via the Nox/Src42A-dependent pathway.
source: These data are consistent with the possibility that actin released into the haemolymph after septic injury can trigger JAK/STAT activation in the fat body via the Nox/Src42A-dependent pathway described here.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing actin release during septic injury and requirement for Nox/Src42A in the TotM response.

claim: Sterile inflammation is initiated by pro-inflammatory signals that are released by damaged cells.
source: The prevailing notion is that sterile inflammation is initiated by pro-inflammatory signals that are released by damaged cells. These include intracellular components that are exposed when cells lose their membrane integrity, such as ATP, uric acid, RNA and DNA, collectively known as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) (Rock et al., 2010; Zelenay and Reis e Sousa, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rock et al., 2010; Zelenay and Reis e Sousa, 2013).

claim: DAMPs include intracellular components that are exposed when cells lose their membrane integrity, such as ATP, uric acid, RNA and DNA.
source: The prevailing notion is that sterile inflammation is initiated by pro-inflammatory signals that are released by damaged cells. These include intracellular components that are exposed when cells lose their membrane integrity, such as ATP, uric acid, RNA and DNA, collectively known as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) (Rock et al., 2010; Zelenay and Reis e Sousa, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rock et al., 2010; Zelenay and Reis e Sousa, 2013).

claim: Responses to DAMPs, like responses to microbes, pre-date the vertebrate evolution of T and B cells and have an early metazoan origin.
source: However, it is probable that responses to DAMPs, like responses to microbes, pre-date the vertebrate evolution of T and B cells and have an early metazoan origin, much like the clearance of dead cells (Krysko et al., 2011; Hochreiter-Hufford and Ravichandran, 2013; Eming et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Krysko et al., 2011; Hochreiter-Hufford and Ravichandran, 2013; Eming et al., 2014).

claim: The immune system of Drosophila melanogaster consists of a cellular and a humoural arm, in addition to cell-intrinsic antiviral RNAi responses.
source: The immune system of Drosophila melanogaster has been widely studied in the context of infection. It consists of a cellular and a humoural arm, in addition to cell-intrinsic antiviral RNAi responses (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).

claim: The cellular arm of Drosophila immunity is made up of three macrophage-like types of cells, collectively termed haemocytes.
source: The cellular arm is made up of three macrophage-like types of cells, collectively termed haemocytes (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).

claim: The humoural immune response in Drosophila relies on antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that are synthesised in the fat body and then secreted into the haemolymph.
source: The humoural immune response relies on antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that are synthesised in the fat body (the fly equivalent of the liver) and then secreted into the haemolymph to provide systemic protection from bacteria and fungi (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007; Buchon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007; Buchon et al., 2014).

claim: The production of AMPs in Drosophila is regulated by two different pathways: the Toll pathway and the Imd pathway.
source: The production of AMPs is regulated by two different pathways. The Toll pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments of Gram-positive bacteria, fungal β-glucans, and pathogen-derived protease activity in the haemolymph (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007). The Imd pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments from Gram-negative bacteria (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).

claim: The Toll pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments of Gram-positive bacteria, fungal β-glucans, and pathogen-derived protease activity in the haemolymph.
source: The Toll pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments of Gram-positive bacteria, fungal β-glucans, and pathogen-derived protease activity in the haemolymph (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).

claim: The Imd pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments from Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The Imd pathway is activated by peptidoglycan fragments from Gram-negative bacteria (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila has not yet been shown to be directly induced by sensors of invading microorganisms.
source: A third pathway contributing to Drosophila humoural immunity involves Janus Kinase/Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (JAK/STAT) signalling. In contrast to the Toll and Imd pathway, the JAK/STAT pathway has not yet been shown to be directly induced by sensors of invading microorganisms (Myllymäki and Rämet, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Myllymäki and Rämet, 2014).

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway has been implicated in resistance to as well as tolerance to viral infections.
source: However, it has been implicated in resistance to as well as tolerance to viral infections (Dostert et al., 2005; Lamiable et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Dostert et al., 2005; Lamiable et al., 2016).

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway is activated by different types of stresses (e.g. heat, mechanical pressure, oxidative stress or UV irradiation).
source: Notably, the JAK/STAT pathway is activated by different types of stresses (e.g. heat, mechanical pressure, oxidative stress or UV irradiation) (Lemaitre et al., 1996; Ekengren et al., 2001; Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lemaitre et al., 1996; Ekengren et al., 2001; Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001).

claim: JAK/STAT pathway activation might be triggered by DAMPs rather than microbes.
source: All of these insults likely result in cell death suggesting the possibility that JAK/STAT pathway activation might be triggered by DAMPs rather than microbes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stresses that activate JAK/STAT also cause cell death.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway is elicited by cytokines of the Unpaired (Upd) family – Upd1, Upd2 and Upd3.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway is elicited by cytokines of the Unpaired (Upd) family – Upd1 (Harrison et al., 1998), Upd2 (Gilbert et al., 2005; Hombría et al., 2005) and Upd3 (Agaisse et al., 2003; Wright et al., 2011) – all of which serve as ligands for the only JAK/STAT-coupled receptor in Drosophila, Domeless (dome) (Brown et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Harrison et al., 1998; Gilbert et al., 2005; Hombría et al., 2005; Agaisse et al., 2003; Wright et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2001).

claim: Upd cytokines serve as ligands for the only JAK/STAT-coupled receptor in Drosophila, Domeless.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway is elicited by cytokines of the Unpaired (Upd) family – Upd1 (Harrison et al., 1998), Upd2 (Gilbert et al., 2005; Hombría et al., 2005) and Upd3 (Agaisse et al., 2003; Wright et al., 2011) – all of which serve as ligands for the only JAK/STAT-coupled receptor in Drosophila, Domeless (dome) (Brown et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Brown et al., 2001).

claim: The binding of Upds induces Domeless dimerization and activation of a single JAK (termed Hopscotch).
source: The binding of Upds induces Domeless dimerization and activation of a single JAK (termed Hopscotch).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila.

claim: Activated Hopscotch proteins phosphorylate one another allowing for recruitment of the single Drosophila STAT family transcription factor, STAT92E.
source: Activated Hopscotch proteins phosphorylate one another allowing for recruitment of the single Drosophila STAT family transcription factor, STAT92E.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila.

claim: STAT92E is phosphorylated by Hopscotch, resulting in dimerisation and translocation into the nucleus.
source: The latter is then phosphorylated by Hopscotch, resulting in dimerisation and translocation into the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila.

claim: STAT92E dimers bind to the promoters of their target genes.
source: STAT92E dimers bind to the promoters of their target genes (Kiu and Nicholson, 2012; Bina et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2005) including, amongst others, ones encoding proteins involved in viral resistance (Lamiable et al., 2016; Dostert et al., 2005), as well as proteins of the Turandot family such as Turandot M (TotM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Kiu and Nicholson, 2012; Bina et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2005).

claim: STAT92E target genes include ones encoding proteins involved in viral resistance and proteins of the Turandot family such as Turandot M (TotM).
source: STAT92E dimers bind to the promoters of their target genes (Kiu and Nicholson, 2012; Bina et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2005) including, amongst others, ones encoding proteins involved in viral resistance (Lamiable et al., 2016; Dostert et al., 2005), as well as proteins of the Turandot family such as Turandot M (TotM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lamiable et al., 2016; Dostert et al., 2005).

claim: The exact function of Turandot family proteins is not known.
source: The exact function of Turandot family proteins is not known but they have been controversially argued to be linked to stress resistance (Ekengren and Hultmark, 2001; Ekengren et al., 2001; Mahapatra and Rand, 2012; Zhong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway has been linked to energy metabolism.
source: Besides a role in host defence, the JAK/STAT pathway has also been linked to energy metabolism (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012) and regenerative processes, for example in the gut (Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Jiang et al., 2009).

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway has been linked to regenerative processes, for example in the gut.
source: Besides a role in host defence, the JAK/STAT pathway has also been linked to energy metabolism (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012) and regenerative processes, for example in the gut (Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Jiang et al., 2009).

claim: DNGR-1 is a vertebrate-restricted innate immune receptor dedicated to DAMP recognition.
source: We have previously identified DNGR-1 (also known as CLEC9A) as a vertebrate-restricted innate immune receptor dedicated to DAMP recognition (Sancho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Sancho et al., 2009).

claim: The DAMP recognised by DNGR-1 is F-actin.
source: We and others subsequently found that the DAMP recognised by DNGR-1 is F-actin, the polymer of G-actin that provides higher eukaryotic cells with structural integrity (Ahrens et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ahrens et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Actin is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans).
source: Actin is an ideal DAMP given that it is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans) and highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin conservation.

claim: Actin is highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
source: Actin is an ideal DAMP given that it is extremely conserved (90% identity between yeast and humans) and highly abundant and ubiquitous within all eukaryotic cells but absent from extracellular fluids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin distribution.

claim: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless.
source: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless, a conclusion further supported by the fact that actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirement for Upd3 and supported by in vitro data.

claim: Actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro.
source: The requirement for Upd3 rules out the possibility that actin serves as a direct ligand for Domeless, a conclusion further supported by the fact that actin does not induce TotM upregulation in various Drosophila cell lines that respond to Upd cytokines in vitro (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text as unpublished data.

claim: Upd3 is synthesised by fat body cells that detect extracellular actin via a sensor(s) that couple(s) to a Nox-Src42A-Shark cascade.
source: Therefore, the simplest interpretation of our data is that Upd3 is synthesised by fat body cells that detect extracellular actin via a sensor(s) that couple(s) to a Nox-Src42A-Shark cascade (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a model inferred from the experimental data and depicted in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Drosophila responses to wounding and in the clearance of axonal debris and neuronal cell corpses, Draper is phosphorylated by Src42A.
source: Interestingly, in Drosophila responses to wounding and in the clearance of axonal debris and neuronal cell corpses, one such receptor is Draper, a member of the Nimrod family and orthologue of C. elegans Ced1. Draper contains an ITAM that is phosphorylated by Src42A (MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2008; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (MacDonald et al., 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2008; Razzell et al., 2013; Evans et al., 2015).

claim: The fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin.
source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2k and 2l.

claim: The fly response to extracellular actin does not require phagocytes but the fat body.
source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing haemocytes are dispensable (Figure 5) and the fat body is required (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: The function of the fly response to extracellular actin is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
source: In contrast to DNGR-1 dependent recognition, the fly response to extracellular actin is elicited equally by G- and F-actin, does not require phagocytes but the fat body and its function is not to prime adaptive immunity, which is absent in invertebrates.
evidence: This is based on the established knowledge that invertebrates lack adaptive immunity.

claim: The fly response to extracellular actin is coupled to production of Upd3 cytokine, which acts in an autocrine and paracrine manner to induce Domeless signalling via STAT.
source: Rather, it is coupled to production of Upd3 cytokine, which acts in an autocrine and paracrine manner to induce Domeless signalling via STAT and to cause the induction of STAT-responsive genes, the products of which are released into the haemolymph.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The Drosophila fat body response to actin results in secretion into the haemolymph of proteins that may regulate multiple aspects of fly physiology.
source: Similarly, the Drosophila fat body response to actin results in secretion into the haemolymph of proteins that may regulate multiple aspects of fly physiology that coordinately impact resistance or tolerance to insult.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of STAT target genes and the analogy to the mammalian acute phase response.

claim: Some components of the extracellular actin-sensing circuitry are conserved between flies and mammals (Shark, Src42A and ROS), while others are not (DNGR1, cross-presentation, dendritic cells).
source: However, it is important to note that while some components of the extracellular actin-sensing circuitry are conserved between flies and mammals (Shark, Src42A and ROS), others are not (DNGR1, cross-presentation, dendritic cells).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the fly and mammalian systems.

claim: DAMPs can be more conserved than their receptors or the responses they evoke.
source: These differences suggest that DAMPs can be more conserved than their receptors or the responses they evoke.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that actin is conserved but the receptors and responses differ between flies and mammals.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila can be induced by mechanical pressure, heat shock, dehydration, cytopathic infection, septic wounds and other traumas.
source: The JAK/STAT pathway in Drosophila can be induced by mechanical pressure, heat shock, dehydration, cytopathic infection, septic wounds and other traumas (Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Dostert et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Ekengren et al., 2001; Agaisse et al., 2003; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Dostert et al., 2005).

claim: A common denominator in all stimuli that induce JAK/STAT is cell death.
source: How such seemingly disparate stimuli trigger a single pathway is puzzling. However, a common denominator in all these settings is cell death and it has been speculated that STAT activation might therefore occur in response to DAMP release (Shaukat et al., 2015; Buchon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all JAK/STAT-inducing stimuli cause cell death, and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Actin is a potent DAMP for triggering the JAK/STAT pathway.
source: Our data support that notion and suggest that actin is a potent DAMP for triggering the JAK/STAT pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing actin induces JAK/STAT activation.

claim: Pathogen infection in Anopheles gambiae and Drosophila melanogaster has been shown to lead to the release of actin into the haemolymph.
source: Notably, pathogen infection in Anopheles gambiae and Drosophila melanogaster has been shown to lead to the release of actin into the haemolymph, where it can act as an antibacterial or antiparasitic agent (Vierstraete et al., 2004; Sandiford et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Vierstraete et al., 2004; Sandiford et al., 2015).

claim: Actin in the haemolymph can act as an antibacterial or antiparasitic agent.
source: Notably, pathogen infection in Anopheles gambiae and Drosophila melanogaster has been shown to lead to the release of actin into the haemolymph, where it can act as an antibacterial or antiparasitic agent (Vierstraete et al., 2004; Sandiford et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Vierstraete et al., 2004; Sandiford et al., 2015).

claim: Actin release may serve as a two-pronged defense mechanism, both directly as an antimicrobial and indirectly by activating a systemic JAK/STAT response.
source: Therefore, actin release may serve as a two-pronged defense mechanism, both directly as an antimicrobial and indirectly by activating a systemic JAK/STAT response.
evidence: This is inferred from the known antimicrobial activity of actin and the data showing actin activates JAK/STAT.

claim: Genetic loss-of-function studies have implicated JAK/STAT signaling in resistance and/or tolerance to viral, bacterial and parasitoid infections.
source: Despite being commonly used as a marker of STAT activation, the function of Tot and Tep proteins in Drosophila is unknown. Nevertheless, genetic loss-of-function studies have implicated JAK/STAT signaling in resistance and/or tolerance to viral, bacterial and parasitoid infections (Yang et al., 2015; Agaisse et al., 2003; Agaisse and Perrimon, 2004; Brun et al., 2006; Dostert et al., 2005; Lamiable et al., 2016; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Kemp et al., 2013; Merkling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Yang et al., 2015; Agaisse et al., 2003; Agaisse and Perrimon, 2004; Brun et al., 2006; Dostert et al., 2005; Lamiable et al., 2016; Chakrabarti et al., 2016; Kemp et al., 2013; Merkling et al., 2015).

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway has a well-established role in maintenance of fly intestinal homeostasis, both at steady state and following infection or injury.
source: Furthermore, the JAK/STAT pathway has a well-established role in maintenance of fly intestinal homeostasis, both at steady state and following infection or injury (Biteau et al., 2011; Kohlmaier et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2009; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Zhou et al., 2013; Osman et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2011; Beebe et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010; Zhai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Biteau et al., 2011; Kohlmaier et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2009; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Zhou et al., 2013; Osman et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2011; Beebe et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010; Zhai et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of basal Diedel levels leads to reduced tolerance to Sindbis virus, yet the upregulation of Diedel levels that takes place during infection is itself dispensable.
source: Reinforcing this notion is a recent study showing that loss of basal Diedel levels leads to reduced tolerance to Sindbis virus, yet the upregulation of Diedel levels that takes place during infection is itself dispensable (Lamiable et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work (Lamiable et al., 2016).

claim: ROS generation by NADPH oxidases is a highly conserved response to wounding.
source: Consistent with our data, ROS generation by NADPH oxidases is a highly conserved response to wounding (Nam et al., 2012; Takeishi et al., 2013) and has been shown to directly activate Lyn/Src42A in zebrafish and Drosophila through oxidation of a single redox-sensitive cysteine residue (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2015; Razzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Nam et al., 2012; Takeishi et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2015; Razzell et al., 2013).

claim: NADPH oxidases have been shown to directly activate Lyn/Src42A in zebrafish and Drosophila through oxidation of a single redox-sensitive cysteine residue.
source: Consistent with our data, ROS generation by NADPH oxidases is a highly conserved response to wounding (Nam et al., 2012; Takeishi et al., 2013) and has been shown to directly activate Lyn/Src42A in zebrafish and Drosophila through oxidation of a single redox-sensitive cysteine residue (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2015; Razzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Yoo et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2009; Evans et al., 2015; Razzell et al., 2013).
